questionText: A supply air temperature that continuously oscillates 3°F above and below setpoint without stabilizing indicates:

choices.text: Hunting — the cooling valve PID loop's integral gain is too aggressive
Normal operation, since temperature always varies around setpoint
A stuck cooling valve that cannot hold position
Incorrect minimum airflow setpoints causing load fluctuations

explanation: Hunting is caused by an overly aggressive control loop, typically excessive integral gain. The fix is reducing gain (increasing integral time) until the loop stabilizes.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Building Automation Systems and Controls Commissioning

category: Building Automation Systems and Controls Commissioning
subcategory: Controls Commissioning Issues and PID Tuning
questionText: Documenting as-found and as-left setpoints during commissioning serves to:

choices.text: Provide a verified reference for future operators, so unauthorized or unintended deviations can be identified years later
Satisfy OSHA documentation requirements for HVAC work
Create a record for the controls contractor's warranty claim
Allow the CxA to bill for setpoint correction separately from functional testing

explanation: Setpoint documentation creates a permanent baseline — years later, comparing current settings against the commissioning record quickly identifies drift or unauthorized changes.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Building Automation Systems and Controls Commissioning

category: Building Automation Systems and Controls Commissioning
subcategory: Controls Commissioning Issues and PID Tuning
questionText: A smoke detector wired to a DDC input with no programmed response is a commissioning deficiency because:

choices.text: The AHU won't shut down on smoke detection — a life-safety failure that looks correct on a wiring diagram
Wiring smoke detectors to DDC is not allowed by code
The CxA is required to program all DDC sequences
A smoke detector input increases complexity without safety benefit

explanation: Wiring without programming is a common but dangerous deficiency — hardware is present, but no software action triggers, so the AHU keeps running in a fire event despite the wiring diagram looking correct.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Building Automation Systems and Controls Commissioning

category: Building Automation Systems and Controls Commissioning
subcategory: Controls Commissioning Issues and PID Tuning
questionText: The most common controls deficiency type found in new construction commissioning is:

choices.text: Incorrect setpoints — values programmed differently than specified
Physical actuator failures during construction
Sensor wiring errors to the wrong DDC input
Protocol incompatibilities between manufacturers

explanation: Setpoint errors — especially minimum airflow, temperature reset range, and deadband values — are the most frequently found deficiency type in new construction commissioning.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Building Automation Systems and Controls Commissioning

category: Building Automation Systems and Controls Commissioning
subcategory: Controls Commissioning Issues and PID Tuning
questionText: Step testing, as a PID tuning verification method, involves:

choices.text: Changing the setpoint by a known amount and observing the response
Replacing the physical valve actuator entirely
Only reviewing the manufacturer's default PID values
Waiting one full year to observe seasonal drift

explanation: Step testing is the most straightforward tuning verification — a known setpoint change reveals whether the loop responds appropriately without hunting, sluggishness, or offset.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Building Automation Systems and Controls Commissioning

category: Building Automation Systems and Controls Commissioning
subcategory: Controls Commissioning Issues and PID Tuning
questionText: A sluggish PID loop, taking minutes or hours to reach setpoint, is typically caused by:

choices.text: Insufficient gain
Excessive integral gain
A perfectly tuned loop with no issue
A physically oversized actuator

explanation: Sluggish response — the opposite problem from hunting — comes from insufficient gain, where the loop responds too weakly to reach setpoint in a reasonable time.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Building Automation Systems and Controls Commissioning

category: Building Automation Systems and Controls Commissioning
subcategory: Controls Commissioning Issues and PID Tuning
questionText: Missing sequences, as a controls deficiency category, refers to:

choices.text: A specified operating mode — like morning warm-up or night setback — not programmed at all
A sequence that runs correctly but at the wrong time of day
A sequence documented in the O&M manual but not in the specification
A sequence tested successfully but not yet trended

explanation: Missing sequences occur when the controls contractor omits a specified mode entirely, often because a standard programming template didn't include it — a gap the CxA's SOO verification catches.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Building Automation Systems and Controls Commissioning

category: Building Automation Systems and Controls Commissioning
subcategory: Controls Commissioning Issues and PID Tuning
questionText: An offset in a PID loop (the controlled variable settles near but not at setpoint) is commonly caused by:

choices.text: Missing integral action
Excessive derivative gain
A correctly tuned loop functioning as designed
A sensor calibration error only

explanation: Without integral action, a proportional-only control loop typically settles at some residual error (offset) rather than driving all the way to the exact setpoint.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Building Automation Systems and Controls Commissioning

category: Building Automation Systems and Controls Commissioning
subcategory: Controls Commissioning Issues and PID Tuning
questionText: 'Wired but not programmed' as a deficiency category describes:

choices.text: An input physically connected to the DDC controller with no corresponding action programmed in response
A device that has no physical wiring at all
A sequence programmed correctly but never tested
A point that exists only in the operator workstation graphics, not in reality

explanation: This deficiency type — hardware present, software response missing — is deceptively easy to miss on paper, since a wiring diagram alone can't reveal that no logic responds to the input.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Building Automation Systems and Controls Commissioning

category: Building Automation Systems and Controls Commissioning
subcategory: Controls Commissioning Issues and PID Tuning
questionText: PID tuning is usually performed by the controls contractor, while the CxA's role is to:

choices.text: Verify the tuning result, typically by examining trend data for hunting or offset after adjustments are made
Perform all tuning personally with no contractor involvement
Skip tuning verification entirely, since it's outside the Cx scope
Only verify tuning during the pre-design phase, before any equipment is installed

explanation: The division of labor is clear — the controls contractor tunes the loops, and the CxA independently verifies the result holds up under trend data review or step testing.
referenceBookSection: Module 4 — Building Automation Systems and Controls Commissioning

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: LEED Commissioning Requirements
questionText: For LEED EA Prerequisite — Fundamental Commissioning, the CxA:

choices.text: Can be a qualified member of the project team — independence is not required at this level
Must be completely independent of the design team and GC
Must hold the BCxP certification from ACG
Must be a licensed mechanical engineer in the project state

explanation: EA Prerequisite allows the CxA to be from the design or construction team. Independence becomes a requirement only at the EA Credit — Enhanced Commissioning level.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: LEED Commissioning Requirements
questionText: LEED EA Credit — Enhanced Commissioning adds what requirement beyond the prerequisite?

choices.text: Independent CxA, comprehensive multi-stage design reviews, systems manual, and a 10-month post-occupancy review
Additional TAB measurements at post-occupancy
A third-party energy audit comparing modeled vs actual energy use
Monthly BAS review by the CxA for the first year after occupancy

explanation: Enhanced Cx adds independence, multi-stage design reviews (schematic through construction documents), a systems manual, submittal review, and a 10-month post-occupancy review — with MBCx at the top tier.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: LEED Commissioning Requirements
questionText: A technically excellent commissioning process with incomplete LEED documentation submittals may result in:

choices.text: Credit denial, since GBCI reviewers verify documentation completeness regardless of technical quality
A reduced but nonzero point award proportional to documentation completeness
No impact, since GBCI accepts verbal confirmation from the CxA
A standard 90-day extension to complete documentation

explanation: LEED credit is documentation-dependent — if the paperwork doesn't demonstrate the required process was followed, the credit is denied regardless of how well the actual commissioning work was performed.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: LEED Commissioning Requirements
questionText: LEED documentation submitted to GBCI for commissioning includes:

choices.text: The OPR, BOD, commissioning plan, design review comments, PCLs, FPT results, issues log, and final report
Only a one-page summary letter from the CxA
Only the construction cost estimate
Only the building's floor plans

explanation: GBCI requires the full commissioning documentation set to verify the process was actually followed — a comprehensive package, not a summary.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: LEED Commissioning Requirements
questionText: The back-check step in LEED fundamental commissioning verifies:

choices.text: That design review comments were actually addressed
The building's structural load calculations
The contractor's payment application accuracy
The building's parking ratio compliance

explanation: A back-check confirms design review comments weren't just noted but actually incorporated into the revised design — closing the loop on the review process.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: LEED Commissioning Requirements
questionText: Monitoring-Based Commissioning (MBCx) is required for:

choices.text: The top tier of Enhanced Commissioning (EA Credit, Option 2)
Every LEED project regardless of certification level
Only projects seeking LEED Platinum with no other pathway
Only projects under 10,000 square feet

explanation: MBCx is a requirement of the top enhanced tier, not a universal LEED requirement — building on the base commissioning scope with ongoing automated monitoring.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: LEED Commissioning Requirements
questionText: For EA Prerequisite, the CxA must:

choices.text: Develop a commissioning plan before design development and review the OPR
Complete a 10-month post-occupancy review, same as Enhanced Cx
Hold a state-issued mechanical engineering license
Have no involvement until after occupancy begins

explanation: Even the base prerequisite requires early involvement — a commissioning plan before design development and OPR review — distinct from the deeper Enhanced Cx requirements like the post-occupancy review.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: LEED Commissioning Requirements
questionText: LEED EA Credit — Building-Level Energy Metering requires:

choices.text: Whole-building electrical energy metering with data shared for ongoing performance verification
Only a one-time energy audit at project completion
Metering exclusively of the HVAC system, excluding lighting and plug loads
No metering requirement — energy use is estimated via modeling only

explanation: This credit requires ongoing whole-building metering, not a one-time snapshot — the CxA often assists verifying the metering system is correctly installed and communicating to the monitoring platform.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: LEED Commissioning Requirements
questionText: Comprehensive design review under Enhanced Commissioning occurs at:

choices.text: Schematic design, design development, and construction documents stages
Only the construction documents stage
Only after the building has been occupied for one year
Only at the very final punch list walkthrough

explanation: Enhanced Cx design review spans multiple design stages, catching issues progressively earlier than a single late-stage review would.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: LEED Commissioning Requirements
questionText: GBCI reviewers examining commissioning documentation are primarily checking whether:

choices.text: The documented process was actually followed
The building's final sale price exceeds a minimum threshold
The CxA personally holds a PE license
The building uses a specific brand of BAS hardware

explanation: GBCI's review focuses on process compliance as evidenced by documentation — confirming the required commissioning activities actually occurred, in the required sequence, with the required records.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: Enclosure Commissioning and Energy Performance Verification
questionText: A blower door test measures a building's:

choices.text: Whole-building air leakage at a standard pressure differential (50 Pa), expressed as ACH50 or CFM50
Overall thermal resistance of the building envelope
Air distribution balance across all conditioned spaces
Mechanical ventilation effectiveness per ASHRAE 62.1

explanation: A fan pressurizes or depressurizes the building to 50 Pa, and the airflow required to maintain that pressure directly quantifies whole-building air leakage.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: Enclosure Commissioning and Energy Performance Verification
questionText: Infrared thermography during enclosure commissioning is most effective when:

choices.text: There is a temperature differential of at least 10°F and the building is depressurized with a blower door
Performed at midday with maximum solar gain on exterior surfaces
The building is at uniform indoor temperature
Performed at night with the HVAC system shut down

explanation: Thermal imaging needs a real temperature differential to create contrast, and blower door depressurization forces air through gaps to make them thermally visible.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: Enclosure Commissioning and Energy Performance Verification
questionText: Air barrier continuity is a common design deficiency because:

choices.text: Continuity details at penetrations, transitions, and structural connections are often not explicitly designed
Air barriers are voluntary and most designers omit them entirely
Air barriers are only required for residential construction
Standard specification language covers all continuity details automatically

explanation: The gaps that undermine air barrier performance typically occur at penetrations and transitions between systems (wall to roof, wall to slab) — details often left incomplete in design documents.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: Enclosure Commissioning and Energy Performance Verification
questionText: Building Envelope Commissioning (BECx) applies the commissioning process to:

choices.text: The building's thermal and moisture envelope — walls, roofs, windows, doors, air barriers, and vapor retarders
Only the electrical distribution system
Only the fire alarm system
Only the elevator system

explanation: BECx extends commissioning discipline to the building's enclosure — a high-impact but historically under-verified element of construction.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: Enclosure Commissioning and Energy Performance Verification
questionText: Testing air leakage before enclosure close-out, rather than post-occupancy, is preferred because:

choices.text: Remediation is still feasible before the enclosure is sealed and finished
Blower door testing cannot physically be performed after occupancy
Pre-close-out testing is required by ASHRAE 90.1 with no exceptions
There is no meaningful difference in when the test is performed

explanation: Testing before close-out means any deficiencies found can still be corrected while access to the enclosure assembly remains practical — far more effective than discovering problems after finishes are complete.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: Enclosure Commissioning and Energy Performance Verification
questionText: A thermal image alone, without interpretive analysis, is:

choices.text: Not a complete commissioning deliverable — a trained thermographer's interpretation is required
A fully sufficient commissioning deliverable on its own
Only useful for marketing materials, not technical documentation
Automatically analyzed by the camera with no human review needed

explanation: Raw thermal images require expert interpretation to distinguish real deficiencies (insulation voids, thermal bridges, moisture) from normal thermal variation — the analysis is what makes the image useful.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: Enclosure Commissioning and Energy Performance Verification
questionText: The OPR should include enclosure performance requirements such as:

choices.text: Target ACH50, target U-values for windows and walls, and air barrier continuity requirements
Only the exterior paint color specification
Only the landscape irrigation schedule
Only the parking structure's load rating

explanation: Enclosure performance targets belong in the OPR alongside HVAC and other system requirements, since enclosure performance directly affects energy use and comfort — core OPR concerns.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: Enclosure Commissioning and Energy Performance Verification
questionText: The building enclosure is described in the training as:

choices.text: One of the highest-impact determinants of building performance but also one of the least systematically verified elements of construction
A low-impact system with negligible effect on energy use
A system that requires no commissioning attention since it is passive
The most rigorously verified system in typical construction practice

explanation: This gap between the enclosure's real impact and how little it's typically verified is exactly why building envelope commissioning has grown as a distinct discipline.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: Enclosure Commissioning and Energy Performance Verification
questionText: During construction, the CxA's enclosure commissioning activities include:

choices.text: Witnessing mock-up testing of critical enclosure assemblies and reviewing contractor QC procedures
Only reviewing the final as-built survey after occupancy
Only approving the exterior finish color selections
Only inspecting the roofing warranty documentation

explanation: Mock-up testing of critical assemblies, witnessed by the CxA, catches enclosure problems while they're still correctable across the whole building — before the full assembly is replicated.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: Enclosure Commissioning and Energy Performance Verification
questionText: ASHRAE 90.1-2019 includes requirements addressing:

choices.text: Air leakage
Only elevator dispatch algorithms
Only parking garage ventilation
Only emergency generator fuel storage

explanation: ASHRAE 90.1-2019 includes air leakage requirements, while LEED and Passive House standards go further with more stringent thresholds for enclosure performance.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: Final Commissioning Report and Ongoing Commissioning Programs
questionText: The executive summary of the final commissioning report should be written for:

choices.text: Building owners and facility managers, clearly stating what was found, fixed, and deferred
A detailed technical audience organized system-by-system with full test data
A legal certification that all systems meet ASHRAE requirements
An exact copy of the commissioning plan with no updates

explanation: The executive summary must be readable by a facilities manager without deep HVAC technical knowledge — clarity builds the CxA's value more than technical depth in this particular section.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: Final Commissioning Report and Ongoing Commissioning Programs
questionText: The recommended recommissioning cycle for a commissioned building is approximately:

choices.text: Every 5–7 years
Annually, without exception
Only upon ownership change or major renovation
Commissioning is permanent and requires no repeat

explanation: Systems drift from their commissioned baseline over years — setpoints change, sensors drift, actuators wear. A 5–7 year cycle catches this before it significantly affects performance.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: Final Commissioning Report and Ongoing Commissioning Programs
questionText: The economic return on retro-commissioning existing buildings is particularly compelling because:

choices.text: Simple payback averages approximately 1 year from energy savings alone
Federal tax credits offset 50% of retro-Cx costs automatically
Retro-Cx costs are typically covered by the mechanical contractor's warranty
Energy savings from retro-Cx are guaranteed by the CxA for 5 years

explanation: PECI/LBNL research shows average retro-Cx payback of approximately 1.1 years, driven largely by low-cost or free software/controls corrections rather than capital equipment replacement.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: Final Commissioning Report and Ongoing Commissioning Programs
questionText: New construction commissioning typically costs what share of construction costs?

choices.text: Commissioning has no measurable cost impact on construction budgets

explanation: This small investment (0.5–1.5% of construction) is what typically yields 8–15% energy savings — one of the highest-ROI investments in the building industry.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: Final Commissioning Report and Ongoing Commissioning Programs
questionText: Ongoing monitoring-based commissioning (MBCx) programs prevent:

choices.text: The 15–30% performance degradation commissioned buildings experience without ongoing monitoring
All future equipment failures, fully replacing preventive maintenance
LEED certification lapses after 5 years
All occupant complaints automatically

explanation: Commissioned buildings gradually revert toward non-commissioned performance without ongoing monitoring — MBCx catches this drift early, before it compounds.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: Final Commissioning Report and Ongoing Commissioning Programs
questionText: The final commissioning report includes:

choices.text: The scope of commissioning, FPT results summary, issues log status, training completed, and a recommissioning recommendation
Only the total commissioning fee invoice
Only the building's certificate of occupancy
Only the general contractor's punch list

explanation: The final report is the capstone document summarizing the entire commissioning effort — scope, status of every deliverable, and a forward-looking recommissioning recommendation.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: Final Commissioning Report and Ongoing Commissioning Programs
questionText: Ongoing MBCx costs, per square foot per year, are approximately:

choices.text: MBCx has no ongoing cost once the initial system is installed

explanation: At this modest annual cost, ongoing MBCx prevents the substantial performance degradation that would otherwise occur — a favorable long-term economic trade-off.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: Final Commissioning Report and Ongoing Commissioning Programs
questionText: Owners who invest in ongoing commissioning programs, versus treating commissioning as one-time, see:

choices.text: Consistently lower energy costs, fewer equipment failures, and better occupant satisfaction
No measurable difference in outcomes
Higher costs with no corresponding benefit
Improved outcomes only in the first year, with no lasting benefit

explanation: Treating commissioning as an ongoing program rather than a one-time event compounds the initial investment's value over the building's lifetime.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: Final Commissioning Report and Ongoing Commissioning Programs
questionText: New construction commissioning typically yields energy savings of approximately:

choices.text: 8–15% versus non-commissioned buildings
New construction commissioning yields no measurable energy savings

explanation: This 8–15% savings, combined with the modest 0.5–1.5% construction cost premium, produces the 2–5 year simple payback that makes new construction commissioning such a strong investment.
referenceBookSection: Module 5 — LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation

category: LEED Commissioning Credits and Final Documentation
subcategory: Final Commissioning Report and Ongoing Commissioning Programs
questionText: A jargon-heavy final commissioning report is a problem because:

choices.text: Reports that aren't read don't build the CxA's value or referral relationship with the owner
GBCI automatically rejects reports containing technical terminology
Jargon-heavy reports violate ASHRAE Guideline 0 formatting requirements
There is no practical downside to a jargon-heavy report

explanation: A report the owner never actually reads fails to deliver the CxA's value, regardless of how thorough the underlying technical work was — readability is a practical business consideration, not just a style preference.
